A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same hierarchical vision-language segmentation framework, renamed from HierVL to HVL. All 12 pages of v1 and 13 pages of v2, including figures, equations, tables and references, support comparison. Neither PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation results on four datasets, class-wise scores, component and regularization ablations, and qualitative predictions.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and reports additional backbone results and revised ablation results.

M1.justification: Section 3 adds an explicit diversity loss between hierarchical query levels. It also describes direct query-pixel mask products in place of v1's MLP-generated mask kernels. These are local revisions within the retained hierarchical-query, bidirectional-alignment and dual-query architecture; HSQG-to-HTQG and CMSAM-to-PTRM renaming alone does not establish a method change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate semi-supervised semantic segmentation on Pascal VOC, COCO, ADE20K and Cityscapes. The represented datasets, class coverage and tasks remain unchanged; neither introduces an actual domain-shift evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds UniMatch-v2 with DINOv2-S and DINOv2-B alongside the retained comparators across the four benchmarks. The component ablation also replaces its SemiVL reference with a randomly initialized-query Mask2Former baseline. These changes substantially revise the comparison against prior methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds EVA02-L with 14-pixel patches to the original CLIP ViT-B/16 configuration. Section 4.1 changes the reported dataset-specific base learning rates to a uniform 0.0001, while retaining the labeled splits, crop sizes and epoch budgets. It states both polynomial and linear decay, leaving the precise schedule inconsistent. These reported setting changes do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: The component ablation changes from testing additions to SemiVL to testing textual semantic queries against randomly initialized Mask2Former queries. Later component rows, the class-wise ablation and the regularization comparisons retain their results. The qualitative cases are redistributed across figures, without adding new test cases or robustness analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The segmentation results remain point estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains the original ViT-B/16 scores but adds EVA02-L and UniMatch-v2 results across the benchmarks. For example, COCO with 232 labels gains a newly reported EVA02-L score of 59.4 alongside the retained ViT-B/16 score of 54.5; this is not a same-setting improvement. The ablation reference changes from 84.0/87.3 to 82.0/83.3, while class-wise and regularization scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a mathematical definition of cross-level query diversity using squared cosine similarity. v1's separate squared-distance query-to-text alignment objective is no longer specified. The prompt-topology, anchor and masked-consistency formulations remain substantially equivalent; no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central claim of label-efficient, language-guided segmentation remains. However, v2's abstract and introduction emphasize semantic pixel grouping and class discrimination, dropping v1's explicit headline promises of preventing instance collapse and cleanly separating overlapping objects. The introduction also states a more specific first-use claim for image-adapted textual object queries in semi-supervised segmentation.

C2.justification: v2 develops an interpretation of textual queries as semantic cluster centers and explains instance queries as helping group diverse appearances into the same class. v1 emphasizes spatial grounding and separation of overlapping instances. The limitation concerning inherited CLIP biases and poorly represented domain-specific classes remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents six pixel-decoder layers, 1,500 warm-up iterations and rare-class sampling, and changes reported hardware from one to two RTX-3090 GPUs. Conversely, it removes v1's numerical regularization weights, temperature value, module-specific learning-rate multiplier and sliding-window overlap specification. These additions and omissions substantially change reproducibility information without proving that every newly documented practice is new.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused toward semi-supervised learning and query design, with detailed positioning against SemiVL, UniMatch-v2 and Mask2Former. Newly discussed works include kMaX-DeepLab, MP-Former and MDETR, while earlier discussions and references covering LXMERT, ViLBERT, VisualBERT, OpenSeg and LSeg disappear. This goes beyond citation-format changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method narrative are extensively rewritten. Numbered method subsections become component paragraphs, many displayed equations move inline, terminology changes throughout, and the conclusion is substantially compressed. Citations also change from numbered references to author-year style.

P2.justification: The architecture diagram is substantially redrawn with staged components and a separate attention panel. v1's qualitative Figure 4 is split and rearranged into v2 Figures 1 and 5 using the same cases. Table 1 gains backbone columns and changes its caption/highlighting convention, while the paired component and regularization ablations become separate tables.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful UniMatch-v2 and EVA02-L comparisons and clearer explanations of semantic grouping. However, it removes important reproducibility settings and introduces conflicting learning-rate schedules. Section 4.2 attributes a 3.4-point Cityscapes gain to UniMatch-v2 although Table 1 provides no result for that comparator at 100 labels; Section 4.3 reports a 5.6-point ablation gain where Table 3 implies 6.6. It is unclear whether the broader evidence outweighs these losses in reproducibility and internal consistency.
